document.title: Advisor-Verifier-Prover Games and the Hardness of Information Theoretic Cryptography

candidate.title: Advisor-Verifier-Prover Protocols Are Lengthy
candidate.subtitle: One hypothesis that would give super-polynomial lower bounds for PIR, secret sharing and garbling at once
candidate.one_line: Every prover-laconic AVP protocol for the class of n-bit predicates needs super-polynomial total communication.
candidate.status_note: Posed as Hypothesis 1.2 and offered 'both as a working hypothesis or as an (ambitious) target for future works'. Theorem 1.3 proves it implies super-polynomial lower bounds on sd-PIR, general secret sharing and fully-decomposable randomized encodings, for none of which a super-linear lower bound is known.
candidate.progress_note: The source adapts counting-based lower bounds to the AVP model, re-deriving several existing bounds in a unified way, and states plainly that it does not reach the best-known bound for any of the primitives.

candidate.why_interesting: A single hypothesis that would settle super-polynomial lower bounds for three primitives at once, in an area where not even super-linear bounds are known and where the three questions are not currently known to relate to each other.
candidate.why_clean: One model, one quantified resource, one quantifier. No cryptographic assumption and no computational bound: all parties are unbounded.

quotes.quote: Every prover-laconic AVP protocol that works for the class of n-bit predicates must have total communication complexity that is super polynomial in n.
Hypothesis 1.2 can be used both as a working hypothesis or as an (ambitious) target for future works.
Under Hypothesis 1.2, sd-PIR over 2n -bit database, SSS over n-bit predicates, and DRE over n-bit predicates have all communication cost that grows super-polynomially in n.
Unfortunately, we do not get the best-known lower bounds for any of the above primitives.
these connections yield a non-trivial AVP with sub-exponential communication complexity of
A major open problem in information-theoretic cryptography is to obtain a super-polynomial lower bound for the communication complexity of basic cryptographic tasks.

check.notes: Hypothesis 1.2 is verbatim on page 4 and Theorem 1.3 sits immediately below it. No repair was needed. Two things were added rather than found: the statement records the source's own $2^{tilde O(sqrt n)}$ prover-laconic AVP as the upper end of the gap, and records that the hypothesis is false without the laconicity restriction, since the source's Example 1.1 gives a non-laconic AVP at polynomial cost. Both are the source's facts, assembled here to show the statement is neither vacuous nor trivially false.
